```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(purrr)
library(tidyr)

theme_set(theme_bw())

timings <- readRDS("results/timings.rds")
monitors <- readRDS("results/monitors.rds")
meta <- readRDS("results/meta.rds")

workers <- meta$workers

wl_label <- c(
  boot_metrics = "A: Bootstrap metrics",
  resample_fit = "B: Resampled model fits",
  perm_importance = "C: Permutation importance",
  boot_pred_interval = "D: Bootstrap prediction intervals"
)

backend_label <- c(
  sequential = "sequential",
  future = "future (multisession)",
  mirai = "mirai",
  mizu = "mizu",
  mizu_stream = "mizu (stream)"
)

backend_cols <- c(
  "future (multisession)" = "#7570B3",
  "mirai" = "#1B9E77",
  "mizu" = "#E7298A",
  "mizu (stream)" = "#F49EC4"
)

bench <- timings |>
  mutate(
    workload = wl_label[workload],
    backend = backend_label[backend]
  )

baseline <- bench |>
  filter(backend == "sequential") |>
  summarize(baseline = mean(elapsed), .by = workload)

par_bench <- bench |>
  filter(backend != "sequential") |>
  inner_join(baseline, by = "workload") |>
  mutate(
    speed_up = baseline / elapsed,
    workload = factor(workload, levels = wl_label),
    backend = factor(backend, levels = backend_label)
  )

# Timing statistics use the three timed runs; the syrup-monitored run
# (which pays the sampler's overhead) is excluded, but is still plotted.
summ <- par_bench |>
  filter(!monitored) |>
  summarize(
    runs = n(),
    mean_elapsed = mean(elapsed),
    sd_elapsed = sd(elapsed),
    mean_speedup = mean(speed_up),
    efficiency = mean_speedup / workers,
    .by = c(workload, backend)
  ) |>
  arrange(workload, desc(mean_speedup))

mon_all <- monitors |>
  mutate(
    workload = wl_label[workload],
    backend = backend_label[backend]
  ) |>
  mutate(rel_time = as.numeric(time - min(time)), .by = c(workload, backend))

mon <- mon_all |>
  filter(pid != main_pid)

busy <- mon |>
  summarize(cores = sum(pct_cpu) / 100, .by = c(workload, backend, rel_time)) |>
  mutate(
    workload = factor(workload, levels = wl_label),
    backend = factor(backend, levels = backend_label)
  )

fmt <- function(x, d = 1) formatC(x, digits = d, format = "f")

get_speedup <- function(wl, be) {
  summ |>
    filter(workload == wl_label[[wl]], backend == backend_label[[be]]) |>
    pull(mean_speedup)
}
get_elapsed <- function(wl, be) {
  summ |>
    filter(workload == wl_label[[wl]], backend == backend_label[[be]]) |>
    pull(mean_elapsed)
}
```

## Overview

This benchmark compares three R parallel backends — **future**
(multisession, via future.apply), **mirai** (local daemons, via
`mirai_map()`), and **mizu** (shared-memory worker pool, via
`mizu_map()`) — on four representative tidymodels workloads. It extends
the methodology of
[topepo/bootstrap-parallel-benchmark](https://github.com/topepo/bootstrap-parallel-benchmark):
same machine for every run, a sequential `lapply()` baseline per
workload, worker CPU utilization sampled with
[syrup](https://github.com/simonpcouch/syrup) at a 50 ms target
interval (~5 Hz realized — each `ps` snapshot costs ~0.15 s), and
correctness verified by comparing every backend's output against the
sequential result.

The workloads are chosen to stress the transport
regimes that separate the backends' architectures: per-task payloads
of growing size (A, B, C), a large read-only input shared across all
tasks (D), and large per-task results (D). All four are standard
modeling workflows, but they are transport-heavy by design — that is
where backend choice matters. Workload D additionally runs a streaming
mizu configuration, whose per-chunk transport mirrors mirai's model
(see Backend calls).

All runs use `r workers` workers on a `r meta$cores`-core Apple Silicon
Mac (R `r sub("R version ", "", meta$r_version)`).

## Workloads

```{r}
#| label: workload-table

tibble(
  Workload = unname(wl_label),
  Tasks = as.integer(meta$n_tasks[names(wl_label)]),
  `Per-task cost` = c("~3 ms", "~45 ms", "~85 ms", "~90 ms"),
  `Per-task input` = c(
    "1 bootstrap split (~200 KB)",
    "1 bootstrap split (~1.7 MB)",
    "1 bootstrap replicate (~2.8 MB)",
    "1 bootstrap split (~3.4 MB)"
  ),
  `Shared input (constant)` = c(
    "—",
    "—",
    "fitted glm (0.2 MB)",
    "38 MB portfolio (250k policies)"
  ),
  `Per-task result` = c(
    "4-row tibble",
    "2-row tibble",
    "30-row tibble",
    "250k-length numeric (2 MB)"
  ),
  `What it represents` = c(
    "bootstrap confidence intervals with yardstick metric sets",
    "fit_resamples() on a parsnip workflow (recipe + logistic regression)",
    "bootstrap permutation importance: 240 replicates, each permuting all 30 predictors in turn",
    "bootstrap prediction intervals: refit a Gamma severity model, score the whole portfolio"
  )
) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Each task function is self-contained — it `require()`s its packages
internally, so no backend-specific package/globals export mechanism is
used, and every backend pays the same worker setup cost:

```r
# A: yardstick metrics on one bootstrap split
task_metrics <- function(split) {
  require(rsample)
  require(yardstick)
  mtr <- metric_set(rmse, rsq, mae, ccc)
  mtr(analysis(split), y, .pred)
}

# B: parsnip workflow fit on the analysis set, scored out-of-bag
task_fit_glm <- function(split) {
  require(rsample); require(recipes); require(parsnip)
  require(workflows); require(yardstick); require(dplyr)
  wf <- workflow() |>
    add_recipe(recipe(class ~ ., data = analysis(split)) |>
                 step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())) |>
    add_model(logistic_reg() |> set_engine("glm"))
  fitted <- fit(wf, data = analysis(split))
  assess <- assessment(split)
  pred <- predict(fitted, assess, type = "prob") |>
    bind_cols(predict(fitted, assess, type = "class")) |>
    bind_cols(assess |> select(class))
  bind_rows(roc_auc(pred, class, .pred_yes),
            accuracy(pred, class, .pred_class))
}

# C: one bootstrap replicate of the validation set; permute each
# predictor in turn and record the AUC drop against the pre-fit model
task_permimp <- function(task, model) {
  require(rsample); require(yardstick); require(dplyr)
  set.seed(task$seed, kind = "Mersenne-Twister")
  dat <- analysis(task$split)
  truth <- dat$y
  pred <- as.numeric(predict(model, newdata = dat, type = "response"))
  base_auc <- roc_auc_vec(truth, pred, event_level = "second")
  cols <- setdiff(colnames(dat), "y")
  importance <- numeric(length(cols))
  for (j in seq_along(cols)) {
    orig <- dat[[cols[j]]]
    dat[[cols[j]]] <- orig[sample.int(length(orig))]
    p <- as.numeric(predict(model, newdata = dat, type = "response"))
    importance[j] <- base_auc - roc_auc_vec(truth, p, event_level = "second")
    dat[[cols[j]]] <- orig
  }
  tibble(col = cols, base_auc = base_auc, importance = importance)
}

# D: refit the severity model on one bootstrap split and predict
# expected loss for every policy in the shared portfolio
task_bootpred <- function(split, portfolio) {
  require(rsample)
  fit <- glm(loss ~ ., data = analysis(split),
             family = Gamma(link = "log"), control = list(maxit = 25))
  as.numeric(predict(fit, newdata = portfolio, type = "response"))
}
```

## Backend calls

The parallel call for each backend, after setup
(`plan(multisession, workers = 12)`, `daemons(12)`,
`mizu_pool(12)` — created once per backend, outside the timed region).
Workload D passes its shared portfolio as a constant argument through
each backend's natural map call (C's only constant is the fitted
model, 0.2 MB):

```r
future.apply::future_lapply(tasks, fn, portfolio = portfolio)
mirai::mirai_map(tasks, fn, .args = list(portfolio = portfolio))[]
mizu::mizu_map(pool, tasks, fn, portfolio = portfolio) |> mizu::mizu_collect()
```

The three handle those constants very differently: future exports them
as globals once per worker chunk **on every call**, mirai serializes
them **with every task**, and mizu stages them **once per call** into
shared memory, where all workers read the same physical pages. mizu's
map is handle-first — `mizu_map()` stages and submits, returning a
`mizu_map` handle immediately, and `mizu_collect()` blocks for the
gathered results (mirai's `[]` collect on `mirai_map()` is the same
two-phase shape). Both halves sit inside the timed region, so the
measured work matches the other backends' blocking maps.

Workload D additionally runs a streaming mizu configuration of the
same map:

```r
# x streams to workers in slices under a sliding window — the split
# list is never staged wholesale; per-chunk payloads, as mirai
mizu::mizu_map(pool, tasks, fn, portfolio = portfolio, .stream = TRUE) |>
  mizu::mizu_collect()
```

The stream arm gives up wholesale staging — the ~1.4 GB split list
never leaves the main process at once — in exchange for bounded
shared-memory use, the same operating point as mirai's dispatcher.
Results still cross as zero-copy views over shared memory.

Per workload and backend: one warmup run (also the correctness check),
three timed runs, and one syrup-monitored run.

::: {.callout-note}
## future.globals.maxSize (historical note)

future before 1.40.0 (April 2025) capped the globals a multisession
plan would export at 500 MiB per future by default, aborting with
*"Will not launch future due to the size of the globals …"* above
it; raising `options(future.globals.maxSize)` was then a required
extra step for large-payload workloads — one the other backends never
needed. Since 1.40.0 the multisession backend defaults to no limit,
and 1.75.0 made `+Inf` the default on every code path, so with the
current future no setting is required: the
`options(future.globals.maxSize = 8 * 1024^3)` in `benchmark.R` is a
harmless remnant of that era.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## mirai: constants, `everywhere()`, and worker RNG

`mirai_map()`'s `...`/`.args` constants are serialized with **every
task** — the measured cost scales linearly with task count (40 tasks
cost ~4× 10 tasks for a 40 MB constant). mirai's documented pattern
for large shared objects is `everywhere()`: one out-of-band export per
daemon, persisted across calls. Measured on these workloads
(export / subsequent map):

- C: `r fmt(meta$extras$perm_importance$export, 2)` s /
  `r fmt(meta$extras$perm_importance$map, 1)` s
- D: `r fmt(meta$extras$boot_pred_interval$export, 2)` s /
  `r fmt(meta$extras$boot_pred_interval$map, 1)` s

C's constant (a 0.2 MB model) is too small for this to matter; D is
the case it exists for. The export amortizes the send side (at 12
serialized copies resident in workers, re-exported whenever the shared
object changes); results still return over sockets, yet on workload D
this is nonetheless the fastest configuration measured (see Findings).

Payload hygiene also matters disproportionately under per-task
serialization: the benchmark's fitted models are stripped to
prediction essentials (butcher-style: no QR matrix, model frame, or
embedded data). An earlier revision of C that shipped an unstripped
glm (~300 MB on 250k rows) as a per-task constant moved ~85 GB per
mirai run, and macOS repeatedly OOM-killed the session (jetsam). The
stripped fits benefit all three backends equally and are standard
practice when deploying a model to workers.

A second difference surfaced in testing: mirai daemons default to the
L'Ecuyer-CMRG RNG while R sessions default to Mersenne-Twister, so a
bare `set.seed()` inside a task produces a *different* stream on mirai
than sequentially or on the other backends; workload C pins
`kind = "Mersenne-Twister"` to keep results comparable.
:::

## Results

Every backend returned results identical to the sequential reference
(`all.equal()` at 1e-8 tolerance) for all four workloads:
`r if (all(unlist(meta$correct))) paste("all", length(meta$correct), "backend × workload combinations match.") else paste("MISMATCH:", names(meta$correct)[!unlist(meta$correct)])`

Elapsed and speed-up statistics are summarized over the three timed
runs; the syrup-monitored run pays the sampler's overhead
(disproportionate on sub-3 s maps) and is excluded from the table, but
its point appears in the speed-up figure and its trace in the CPU
grids below.

```{r}
#| label: results-table

summ |>
  mutate(
    elapsed = sprintf("%.2f ± %.2f", mean_elapsed, sd_elapsed),
    speedup = fmt(mean_speedup, 2),
    efficiency = fmt(100 * efficiency, 0)
  ) |>
  select(
    Workload = workload, Backend = backend, Runs = runs,
    `Elapsed (s)` = elapsed, `Speed-up` = speedup,
    `Efficiency (%)` = efficiency
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "llrrrr")
```

```{r}
#| label: speedups
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5

ggplot(par_bench, aes(backend, speed_up, col = backend)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, lty = 2, col = "red") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = workers, lty = 2, col = "darkgreen") +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.08, alpha = 3 / 4, cex = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~workload) +
  scale_color_manual(values = backend_cols) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Speed-up vs sequential", col = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", axis.text.x = element_blank())
```

Dashed lines: no speed-up (red) and perfect scaling on `r workers`
workers (green). Points include the syrup-monitored run.

## Amdahl's law

[Amdahl's law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amdahl%27s_law) gives the
speed-up from running a workload with parallel fraction $p$ on $n$
workers:

$$S(n) = \frac{1}{(1 - p) + \frac{p}{n}}$$

which saturates at $1 / (1 - p)$ as $n \to \infty$ — the serial
fraction, not the worker count, sets the ceiling:

```{r}
#| label: amdahl-reference
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5

amdahl <- function(n, p) 1 / ((1 - p) + p / n)

expand_grid(n = seq(1, 24, by = 0.25), p = c(0.5, 0.75, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99)) |>
  mutate(speedup = amdahl(n, p), frac = paste0(100 * p, "%")) |>
  ggplot(aes(n, speedup, col = frac)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, lty = 2, col = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 22, y = 22.8, label = "ideal (S = n)", col = "grey40") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 6, 12, 18, 24)) +
  labs(x = "workers", y = "speed-up", col = "parallel fraction") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Inverting the law at each measured `r workers`-worker speed-up gives
the *implied* parallel fraction $p = (1 - 1/S)\,/\,(1 - 1/n)$ of each
backend × workload combination, and the curve that fraction implies
for other worker counts:

```{r}
#| label: amdahl-fits
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6

fits <- summ |>
  mutate(
    p = (1 - 1 / mean_speedup) / (1 - 1 / workers),
    max_speedup = 1 / (1 - p)
  )

imp_serial <- function(wl, be) {
  p <- fits |>
    filter(workload == wl_label[[wl]], backend == backend_label[[be]]) |>
    pull(p)
  100 * (1 - p)
}

curves <- fits |>
  reframe(tibble(n = seq(1, 24, by = 0.25)), .by = c(workload, backend, p)) |>
  mutate(speedup = amdahl(n, p))

labels <- fits |>
  mutate(
    speedup = amdahl(24, p),
    lab = ifelse(
      p >= 0,
      sprintf("%s: %.0f%% parallel (max %.1f×)", backend, 100 * p, max_speedup),
      sprintf("%s: p < 0 (slowdown)", backend)
    )
  ) |>
  arrange(workload, desc(speedup)) |>
  mutate(vj = rep(c(1.4, -0.6), length.out = n()), .by = workload)

ggplot(curves, aes(n, speedup, col = backend)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, lty = 2, col = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(
    data = par_bench, aes(workers, speed_up), alpha = 3 / 4, cex = 1.5,
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, seed = 1)
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = labels,
    aes(24, speedup, label = lab, col = backend, vjust = vj),
    hjust = 1, size = 2.6, show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~workload) +
  scale_color_manual(values = backend_cols) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 6, 12, 18, 24)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.08))) +
  labs(x = "workers", y = "speed-up vs sequential", col = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Each curve passes through the mean of its measured points by
construction — the fit is the inversion at $n = `r workers`$ — so the
plot's content is the asymptote: what workers beyond `r workers`
would buy *if* the serial fraction stayed constant. mizu's curves are
still rising at `r workers` (implied serial fractions
`r fmt(imp_serial("perm_importance", "mizu"), 0)`% on C,
`r fmt(imp_serial("resample_fit", "mizu"), 0)`% on B,
`r fmt(imp_serial("boot_metrics", "mizu"), 0)`% on A), as is mirai's
on C; mirai on A and D is already at its ceiling, where per-task
serialization dominates. future's sub-1 speed-ups on A and D invert
to *negative* parallel fractions — outside the law's domain: the
model assumes a fixed serial share, but the staggered chunk dispatch
behind those runs (see Anomalies) is overhead that grows with worker
count. The flat-below-1 curves are diagnostics of that overhead, not
Amdahl predictions.

### Checking the fit: a worker-count sweep

The fitted curves above are extrapolations from the single
`r workers`-worker measurement. As a check, workloads B and C were
re-run at 2, 4, and 8 workers per backend (`BENCH_SWEEP=1 Rscript
benchmark.R`; same task sets, three timed runs per point, sequential
baseline re-measured in the same session). Solid lines join the
measured mean speed-ups; dotted curves are the Amdahl prediction
pinned at each backend's 12-worker mean — everything left of 12 is the
model predicting measurements it had not seen.

```{r}
#| label: amdahl-sweep
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5

sweep_raw <- readRDS("results/sweep.rds")

sweep <- sweep_raw$timings |>
  mutate(
    workload = wl_label[workload],
    backend = backend_label[backend]
  )

sweep_base <- sweep |>
  filter(backend == "sequential") |>
  summarize(baseline = mean(elapsed), .by = workload)

sweep_meas <- sweep |>
  filter(backend != "sequential") |>
  inner_join(sweep_base, by = "workload") |>
  mutate(
    speed_up = baseline / elapsed,
    workload = factor(workload, levels = wl_label),
    backend = factor(backend, levels = backend_label)
  )

sweep_n <- max(sweep$workers)

# Amdahl prediction pinned at each backend's mean 12-worker speed-up
sweep_pred <- sweep_meas |>
  filter(workers == sweep_n) |>
  summarize(s_top = mean(speed_up), .by = c(workload, backend)) |>
  mutate(p = (1 - 1 / s_top) / (1 - 1 / sweep_n)) |>
  reframe(
    tibble(n = seq(1, sweep_n, by = 0.25)),
    .by = c(workload, backend, p)
  ) |>
  mutate(speedup = amdahl(n, p))

# Karp-Flatt: the implied serial fraction at each worker count —
# constant under Amdahl, drifting when overhead grows with workers
kf <- sweep_meas |>
  summarize(s = mean(speed_up), .by = c(workload, backend, workers)) |>
  mutate(serial = 100 * (1 - (1 - 1 / s) / (1 - 1 / workers)))

kf_serial <- function(wl, be, w) {
  kf |>
    filter(
      workload == wl_label[[wl]],
      backend == backend_label[[be]],
      workers == w
    ) |>
    pull(serial)
}
kf_s <- function(wl, be, w) {
  kf |>
    filter(
      workload == wl_label[[wl]],
      backend == backend_label[[be]],
      workers == w
    ) |>
    pull(s)
}
kf_range <- function(wl, be, w) {
  d <- sweep_meas |>
    filter(
      workload == wl_label[[wl]],
      backend == backend_label[[be]],
      workers == w
    ) |>
    pull(speed_up)
  c(min(d), max(d))
}

ggplot(sweep_meas, aes(workers, speed_up, col = backend)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, lty = 2, col = "grey50") +
  geom_line(data = sweep_pred, aes(n, speedup), lty = 3, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(
    alpha = 1 / 2, cex = 1.2,
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.12, height = 0, seed = 1)
  ) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "line", linewidth = 0.8) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", cex = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~workload) +
  scale_color_manual(values = backend_cols) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2, 4, 8, 12)) +
  labs(x = "workers", y = "speed-up vs sequential", col = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Every backend × worker count returned results identical to the
sequential reference
(`r if (all(unlist(sweep_raw$correct))) "all 24 combinations match" else paste("MISMATCH:", names(sweep_raw$correct)[!unlist(sweep_raw$correct)])`).

If the law held exactly, the implied serial fraction would be the same
at every worker count, so its drift across 2/4/8/12 is the diagnostic
(the Karp–Flatt metric). Measured:

- **mizu** — near-flat:
  `r fmt(kf_serial("resample_fit", "mizu", 2), 1)`→`r fmt(kf_serial("resample_fit", "mizu", 12), 1)`%
  on B,
  `r fmt(kf_serial("perm_importance", "mizu", 2), 1)`→`r fmt(kf_serial("perm_importance", "mizu", 12), 1)`%
  on C, no material trend. The measured points track the fitted curve
  closely:
  the constant-$p$ assumption holds, and mizu's Amdahl curves in the
  previous figure mean what they say.
- **mirai** — *falls* with worker count (B:
  `r fmt(kf_serial("resample_fit", "mirai", 2), 0)`→`r fmt(kf_serial("resample_fit", "mirai", 12), 0)`%,
  C:
  `r fmt(kf_serial("perm_importance", "mirai", 2), 0)`→`r fmt(kf_serial("perm_importance", "mirai", 12), 0)`%):
  its per-task transport is proportionally worst at 2 workers — B
  shows almost no speed-up there
  (`r fmt(kf_s("resample_fit", "mirai", 2), 1)`×) — and amortizes as
  the dispatcher pipelines more workers. The 12-pinned curve therefore
  over-predicts at 2–4 workers.
- **future** — *rises* with worker count (B:
  `r fmt(kf_serial("resample_fit", "future", 2), 0)`→`r fmt(kf_serial("resample_fit", "future", 12), 0)`%,
  C:
  `r fmt(kf_serial("perm_importance", "future", 2), 0)`→`r fmt(kf_serial("perm_importance", "future", 12), 0)`%):
  the overhead-grows-with-workers signature. Measured speed-up peaks
  at 4–8 workers
  (`r fmt(kf_s("resample_fit", "future", 4), 1)`–`r fmt(kf_s("perm_importance", "future", 8), 1)`×)
  and *declines* by 12 as the staggered chunk dispatch (see Anomalies)
  costs more than the added workers return; the Amdahl shape is the
  wrong family here, and the 12-pinned curve under-predicts the
  mid-range. future's 12-worker mean is also the most variable
  quantity in the benchmark:
  `r fmt(kf_s("perm_importance", "future", 12), 1)`× here vs 2.3× in
  the main run, and its three sweep runs on C alone span
  `r fmt(kf_range("perm_importance", "future", 12)[1], 1)`–`r fmt(kf_range("perm_importance", "future", 12)[2], 1)`×
  (a
  `r round(100 * (kf_range("perm_importance", "future", 12)[2] / kf_range("perm_importance", "future", 12)[1] - 1))`%
  spread; mirai and mizu sit within single digits).

The net: the fitted curves are trustworthy only where the serial
fraction is near-flat — mizu on both workloads, and mirai on C from ~8
workers up. Elsewhere the sweep's measured points, not the curves,
are the scaling story.

## CPU utilization

## Per-worker detail (13 grids)

```{r}
#| label: cpu-detail
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| results: asis

detail <- function(wl, be) {
  d <- mon |>
    filter(workload == wl_label[[wl]], backend == backend_label[[be]]) |>
    mutate(worker = factor(pid))
  if (nrow(d) == 0L) {
    return(invisible(NULL))
  }
  ggplot(d, aes(rel_time, pct_cpu, col = worker)) +
    geom_point(cex = 1 / 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1 / 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
    facet_wrap(~worker) +
    labs(
      title = paste(wl_label[[wl]], "—", backend_label[[be]]),
      x = "seconds", y = "CPU (%)"
    )
}

for (wl in names(wl_label)) {
  bes <- if (wl == "boot_pred_interval") {
    c("future", "mirai", "mizu", "mizu_stream")
  } else {
    c("future", "mirai", "mizu")
  }
  for (be in bes) {
    print(detail(wl, be))
  }
}
```
:::

### Anomalies

```{r}
#| label: anomalies-data
#| include: false

cores_mean <- busy |>
  summarize(mean_cores = mean(cores), .by = c(workload, backend))

mc <- function(wl, be) {
  cores_mean |>
    filter(workload == wl_label[[wl]], backend == backend_label[[be]]) |>
    pull(mean_cores)
}
# kernel CPU-seconds per wall-clock second, main process (unmonitored runs)
sysr <- function(wl, be) {
  d <- timings[
    timings$workload == wl & timings$backend == be & !timings$monitored,
  ]
  mean(d$system / d$elapsed)
}
```

Two anomalies stand out in the per-worker grids.

**Staggered dispatch (A and B, future).** Although `future_lapply()`
chunks statically — each worker receives its full share of tasks up
front — the workers are busy in staggered 1–2 s windows that march in
pid order across the run, with only a few computing at any instant:
mean concurrency is `r fmt(mc("boot_metrics", "future"), 1)` of
`r workers` cores in workload A and
`r fmt(mc("resample_fit", "future"), 1)` in B, where mirai and mizu
sustain `r fmt(mc("boot_metrics", "mirai"), 1)` and
`r fmt(mc("boot_metrics", "mizu"), 1)`. The bottleneck is the main
process: it serializes each worker's chunk (~83 MB in A, ~35 MB in B)
and writes the chunks to the workers sequentially over sockets, so a
worker idles until its chunk has fully arrived. This is the saw-tooth
pattern noted in the original benchmark, and it is why future's
speed-ups in A and B fall so far short of the other backends despite
12 workers. mirai's dispatcher streams tasks and mizu's workers read
claimed elements straight off shared pages, so neither shows idle
workers; on A their transport cost appears as total time (mirai) or
not at all (mizu).

**The main process is the transport (D, mirai).** mirai serializes
the shared portfolio with every task, from the main process, before
dispatch: its workers average
`r fmt(mc("boot_pred_interval", "mirai"), 1)` of `r workers` cores —
they idle while the main process serializes ~17 GB of payloads per run
(`r fmt(sysr("boot_pred_interval", "mirai"), 1)` kernel CPU-seconds
per wall-clock second in the main process: socket writes plus the
memory compressor working on daemon heaps that retain task payloads).
mizu's workers sustain `r fmt(mc("boot_pred_interval", "mizu"), 1)`
cores: staging is a single layout write into shared memory, after
which workers read — and publish results — without involving the main
process.

## Findings

```{r}
#| label: findings-data
#| include: false

sp <- function(wl, be) get_speedup(wl, be)
el <- function(wl, be) get_elapsed(wl, be)
```

- **Workload A (5,000 × ~3 ms metric evaluations)** — overhead-bound.
  mizu: `r fmt(sp("boot_metrics", "mizu"), 1)`×
  (`r fmt(el("boot_metrics", "mizu"), 1)` s);
  mirai: `r fmt(sp("boot_metrics", "mirai"), 1)`×;
  future: `r fmt(sp("boot_metrics", "future"), 1)`×.
  mizu stages the ~1 GB split list once into shared memory and workers
  read their claimed elements off the shared pages; the other two
  serialize every task payload to each worker.
- **Workload B (250 × ~45 ms parsnip workflow fits)** — mizu:
  `r fmt(sp("resample_fit", "mizu"), 1)`×, mirai:
  `r fmt(sp("resample_fit", "mirai"), 1)`×, future:
  `r fmt(sp("resample_fit", "future"), 1)`×.
- **Workload C (240 × ~85 ms bootstrap permutation-importance
  replicates)** — larger per-task payloads (~2.8 MB each, ~0.7 GB in
  total). mizu: `r fmt(sp("perm_importance", "mizu"), 1)`×
  (`r fmt(el("perm_importance", "mizu"), 1)` s); mirai:
  `r fmt(sp("perm_importance", "mirai"), 1)`×; future:
  `r fmt(sp("perm_importance", "future"), 1)`×. With the data riding
  per-task payloads instead of a shared constant, mirai's streaming
  dispatch beats future's chunked static dispatch (as in A and B);
  mizu still stages the replicate list once per call and workers read
  their claimed replicates off shared pages.
- **Workload D (400 × ~90 ms bootstrap refits scoring a 250k-policy
  portfolio)** — broadcast in, bulk out. On top of the shared 38 MB
  portfolio, each task returns a 2 MB prediction vector (800 MB
  total): future and mirai unserialize every result byte over sockets,
  while mizu workers publish results into shared memory and the
  collector wraps them as zero-copy views. The two mizu
  configurations separate D's costs. The streaming map —
  `r fmt(sp("boot_pred_interval", "mizu_stream"), 1)`×
  (`r fmt(el("boot_pred_interval", "mizu_stream"), 1)` s,
  `r fmt(mc("boot_pred_interval", "mizu_stream"), 1)` of
  `r workers` worker cores busy) — is fastest by far: the standard
  arm's wholesale staging of the ~1.4 GB split list is a serial
  main-process phase that streaming instead pipelines with execution
  (per-chunk slices under a sliding window), while results still cross
  as zero-copy views. The standard arm manages
  `r fmt(sp("boot_pred_interval", "mizu"), 1)`×
  (`r fmt(el("boot_pred_interval", "mizu"), 1)` s,
  `r fmt(mc("boot_pred_interval", "mizu"), 1)` cores busy). future:
  `r fmt(sp("boot_pred_interval", "future"), 1)`×; mirai:
  `r fmt(sp("boot_pred_interval", "mirai"), 1)`×. Note that the mirai
  figure uses the per-task-constant call: with `everywhere()` (callout
  above) its map drops to
  `r fmt(meta$extras$boot_pred_interval$map, 1)` s — below the staged
  mizu arm but not the streaming one — so D's ranking reflects the
  calling convention, not mirai's ceiling.

The pattern across A→D: the gap between mizu and the socket-based
backends widens as data movement grows relative to compute — per-task
payloads (A, B), shared inputs (C), and large results (D) each add
transport that mizu either does once or never does at all.

## Reproducing

```sh
Rscript benchmark.R                # ~25 min; writes results/*.rds
bash run_all.sh                    # same, but one process per workload with
                                   # per-phase resume (robust to interruption)
BENCH_SWEEP=1 Rscript benchmark.R  # worker-count sweep for B and C;
                                   # writes results/sweep.rds
quarto render benchmark.qmd        # this report
```

Package versions at run time:

```{r}
#| label: versions

tibble(
  package = names(meta$packages),
  version = unname(meta$packages)
) |>
  knitr::kable()
```
